content: Members of the scientific and digital health communities can be considered stakeholders in digital health systems or interventions. These stakeholders may have direct or indirect interests in the products, strategies, data generated, or policies influenced by the digital health intervention. The claims-based approach begins by identifying and listing key stakeholders associated with the project. Digital health projects are typically multidisciplinary and involve a wide range of stakeholders, each contributing different resources and, therefore, having different expectations for returns from the project. Selected stakeholders may represent existing partnerships, those being pursued, or those deemed critical for scaling up. The latter group is particularly important as they can determine whether the digital health intervention will be successfully scaled up. Identifying and including these stakeholders early in the evidence-generation process ensures that the project has sufficient and relevant data to secure buy-in when ready for scale-up. Managers of digital health projects may choose to conduct a formal stakeholder mapping exercise to identify and prioritize relevant stakeholders. The goal of such an exercise is to narrow down the list of stakeholders to those who are considered primary or key stakeholders. Stakeholder categories, their roles, and example claim statements relevant to them can be outlined to guide this process. A common pitfall in synthesizing claim statements is assuming that one knows what stakeholders expect or, worse, assuming that stakeholders have no expectations at all. Clarifying stakeholder expectations early ensures that claim statements are relevant and focused, potentially preventing the allocation of resources to low-priority processes and outcomes. Focus group discussions or in-depth interviews with key informants can be used to gather information on stakeholder perceptions, needs, and expectations. Example questions for stakeholders include: What are the top three priorities for your organization? What are your key expectations from this project? In what ways can this project add value to your organization’s mission? What is the main outcome you expect this digital health intervention to achieve? Stakeholder expectations can then be articulated as claim statements. When articulating claims: Begin by listing all relevant claims for each stakeholder, then narrow them down to the top three most important claims. Avoid vague statements. For example, High-profile innovation improves coverage of the President’s Safe Motherhood Programme is more specific than Innovative project adopted by government. Claim statements may specify processes, outcomes, or health impacts and should ultimately be measurable. Claims can be articulated as specific monitoring and evaluation (M&E) objectives or indicators. Claims can be measured or substantiated during M&E activities. They may also be supported through process documentation, training, content development, fundraising, or the creation of technologies/products. Once claim statements have been measured, it is important to revise them to match the evidence, if needed. For instance, if only a 10% increase in measles vaccination coverage was observed instead of the anticipated 15%, the claim statement must be revised to reflect that statistic. A data-mapping exercise can assist with this process. Examples of claims include: Proactive text message vaccination reminders to mothers improve measles vaccine coverage in their children. Mobile-phone-assisted electronic birth registration is a cost-effective way to enumerate newborns. Providing maternal health information to customers reduces churn and promotes brand loyalty. A digital health supply chain management system allows distribution tracking and verification of drug authenticity from factory to consumers. Frameworks such as conceptual frameworks, results frameworks, logical frameworks, and theories of change are essential tools for monitoring and evaluating digital health interventions. These frameworks help clarify causal relationships, define project goals and objectives, and provide a theoretical basis for the approach. For example: A conceptual framework identifies and illustrates relationships among factors that influence the operation and success of an intervention. A results framework graphically represents a strategy to achieve specific objectives grounded in cause-and-effect logic. A logical framework summarizes what a project intends to do, how it will do it, and how outputs and outcomes will be monitored and evaluated. A theory of change explains how and why desired change is anticipated to occur, linking outcomes and activities in a causal model. These frameworks provide a structured approach to designing, implementing, and evaluating digital health interventions, ensuring that resources are used effectively and that the desired outcomes and impacts are achieved.
